title: World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson (1980)
summary: Oklahoma could not exercise jurisdiction over a New York retailer and its tristate regional distributor merely because the purchasers drove the car into Oklahoma and crashed there; the foreseeability that matters is whether the defendant’s own conduct and connection with the forum are such that it should reasonably anticipate being haled into court there.
notes:
Evaluate each defendant separately. The opinion does not hold that an automobile manufacturer serving Oklahoma would receive the same result, and it does not make a low percentage of forum sales automatically insufficient.

Justice White wrote for a 6–3 Court; Justice Brennan dissented alone, Justice Marshall dissented joined by Justice Blackmun (a retailer joining a national network can expect its product to cause injury elsewhere), and Justice Blackmun dissented separately (automobiles are inherently mobile). The Robinsons bought the Audi from Seaway in 1976 and were driving to Arizona in 1977 when another car struck them.

The often-quoted test is whether the defendant's conduct and connection with the forum are such that it should reasonably anticipate being haled into court there; the manufacturer (Audi) and importer (Volkswagen of America) did not contest Oklahoma jurisdiction, only the regional distributor and the retail dealer did.

sections.Parties: World-Wide Volkswagen Corporation, the New York regional distributor of Volkswagen and Audi vehicles for New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, and Seaway Volkswagen, Inc., the retail dealer in Massena, New York that sold the Robinsons their Audi, were the petitioners. The respondents were Charles S. Woodson, the Creek County district judge whose exercise of jurisdiction they sought to prohibit, Kay Robinson, who was driving and was injured, Harry Robinson, individually and as next friend, and the injured children. Audi NSU, the manufacturer, and Volkswagen of America, the importer, remained defendants in Oklahoma and were not before the Supreme Court.
sections.Material Facts: Harry and Kay Robinson bought a new Audi from Seaway in Massena in 1976 while living in New York. In 1977 the family left New York to make a new home in Arizona. As Kay drove through Oklahoma another car struck the Audi from behind; the gasoline tank ruptured, fire entered the passenger compartment, and Kay and two children were severely burned. World-Wide administered a contractual distribution territory limited to New York, New Jersey and Connecticut; Seaway sold at retail in Massena. Neither closed sales, performed services, kept agents, shipped goods or bought advertising in Oklahoma, and neither received revenue from Volkswagen service centers there. The Robinson Audi was the only car sold by these petitioners shown to have entered Oklahoma, carried there by its purchasers during their move.
sections.Procedural History: The Robinsons sued in the District Court for Creek County, Oklahoma, alleging defective design and placement of the Audi’s fuel tank and fuel system, and joined the manufacturer, importer, distributor and dealer. World-Wide and Seaway appeared specially; the trial court rejected their objection, and they petitioned the Oklahoma Supreme Court for a writ of prohibition. On October 10, 1978 that court assumed original jurisdiction but denied the writ, 585 P.2d 351: it declined to read the place of injury into § 1701.03(a)(3) because § 1701.03(a)(4) separately covered in-state injury from out-of-state acts, and it found (a)(4) satisfied by inferring from the mobility and value of automobiles that the petitioners derived substantial revenue from goods used in Oklahoma. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 440 U.S. 907, treated the objection as preserved despite the petitioners’ loose “venue” language, and reversed 6–3 on January 21, 1980, Justice White writing.
sections.Issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment permit Oklahoma to exercise specific in personam jurisdiction over a New York retailer and a regional distributor whose sales and distribution were confined to the New York–New Jersey–Connecticut market, when their only connection to Oklahoma arose because their customers drove the car through Oklahoma and suffered the accident there?
sections.Holding: No. Due process requires affiliating circumstances created by the defendant itself. World-Wide and Seaway directed no commercial activity toward Oklahoma, and the purchasers’ unilateral transportation of one car supplied the record’s only product entry. The constitutionally relevant foreseeability is not the likelihood that a mobile product will find its way into the forum but whether the defendant’s conduct and connection with the forum are such that it should reasonably anticipate being haled into court there. Justices Brennan, Marshall (joined by Blackmun) and Blackmun dissented; the judgment denying prohibition was reversed, and the claims against Audi and Volkswagen of America remained pending.
sections.Reasoning: The majority identified two functions of the minimum-contacts requirement: protecting the defendant from a distant or inconvenient forum and preserving the territorial allocation of authority among coequal states, so due process can withhold power even where the burden is light and the forum convenient. Once a defendant-created affiliation exists, reasonableness is assessed through the forum’s interest, the plaintiff’s interest in convenient relief, the interstate system’s interest in efficiency and the states’ shared policies; Oklahoma’s accident, witnesses and safety interest could inform fairness but could not create the petitioners’ contacts. Under Hanson the Robinsons’ decision to drive west was unilateral activity attributable to them. A manufacturer or distributor that directly or indirectly cultivates a state’s market and expects consumers there to buy its products, as in Gray, can anticipate suit when the product injures someone there, but these petitioners had confined their selling to the tristate region. The substantial-revenue inference failed because revenue must stem from a cognizable forum contact, and any value from nationwide travel or service centers was too attenuated. Purposeful availment gives sellers advance notice, letting them structure territories, insure and price risk.

learning.why: Oklahoma could not exercise jurisdiction over a New York retailer and regional distributor solely because the purchasers drove the car there and had an accident.

topics.purposeful-availment: The purchasers’ drive into Oklahoma was unilateral movement rather than conduct by these defendants directed to Oklahoma.
topics.cp-stream-commerce: The Court distinguished serving a forum market from a customer carrying a product there.
topics.fairness: Forum interests and litigation convenience did not replace the required defendant-forum relationship.
topics.relatedness: A forum accident alone did not link these regional sellers to the forum.
topics.minimum-contacts: The case is the leading statement that minimum contacts must arise from the defendant's own purposeful conduct, not the unilateral acts of the plaintiff.
topics.specific-jurisdiction: The claim arose from the Oklahoma accident, and the Court held that even a forum-related injury cannot support specific jurisdiction without forum-directed contacts by the defendant.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Brennan dissented (covering this case and Rush v. Savchuk): the accident, hospitalized plaintiffs, witnesses and highway-safety interest were all in Oklahoma, and the petitioners profited from a national highway and dealer system, so a flexible fairness standard should require less defendant contact. Justice Marshall, joined by Justice Blackmun, saw the petitioners as deliberate participants in a nationwide marketing and service network whose product was designed for long-distance travel. Justice Blackmun added that automobiles are uniquely mobile and that Oklahoma’s roads, police and emergency services supported that use.

priorAccount.title: World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson
priorAccount.summary: Oklahoma lacked jurisdiction over the New York retailer and regional distributor on the contacts presented.
priorAccount.notes: Starter brief. Separate the retailer and distributor from the manufacturer and importer. The latter defendants were not the petitioners whose jurisdictional objections the Court decided.

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Seaway, a retailer, and World-Wide Volkswagen, its regional distributor; the underlying plaintiffs were the Robinsons.
sections.Material Facts: The Robinsons bought an Audi in New York and were injured while driving it through Oklahoma. The two petitioners neither served nor sought to serve the Oklahoma market.
sections.Procedural History: The Oklahoma trial court rejected the petitioners’ special appearances. The Oklahoma Supreme Court denied a writ of prohibition. The U.S. Supreme Court reversed.
sections.Issue: Did the car’s foreseeable travel to Oklahoma establish the required connection between these petitioners and the forum?
sections.Holding: No. The forum contacts of these petitioners were insufficient.
sections.Reasoning: The relevant anticipation of suit must follow from the defendant’s own conduct and forum connection. A consumer’s transport of the product did not establish those connections.
